questions.prompt: Today falls inside four nested units of the geologic time scale: the Cenozoic Era, the Holocene Epoch, the Phanerozoic Eon and the Quaternary Period. Arrange them from the longest span of time to the shortest.

items.text: Quaternary Period
items.rationale: Third: a period. The Quaternary covers about the last 2.6 million years and is one of the periods inside the Cenozoic Era.

items.text: Holocene Epoch
items.rationale: Shortest: an epoch. The Holocene covers only about the last twelve thousand years and sits inside the Quaternary Period.

items.text: Phanerozoic Eon
items.rationale: Longest: an eon. The Phanerozoic covers roughly the last 541 million years and holds three whole eras.

items.text: Cenozoic Era
items.rationale: Second: an era. The Cenozoic covers the last 66 million years and is one of the three eras of the Phanerozoic Eon.

questions.explanation: The time scale nests its units like boxes inside boxes: an eon holds eras, an era holds periods, and a period holds epochs. Each name in this "address" for today sits inside the one before it, so each covers less time than the one before.
questions.misconception: Periods or epochs are bigger than eras, or all four units are about the same length.
questions.hint: Picture a set of nesting boxes. Which name is the outermost box?

choices.text: A period inside the Mesozoic Era
choices.rationale: Correct. The Jurassic is listed as a period, between the Triassic and Cretaceous, and all three belong to the Mesozoic Era.

choices.text: A period inside the Cenozoic Era
choices.rationale: Right kind of unit, wrong era. The Cenozoic holds the Paleogene, Neogene and Quaternary, all of them younger than the Jurassic.

choices.text: An era that contains the Triassic and Cretaceous
choices.rationale: The Jurassic sits beside the Triassic and Cretaceous as one of three periods; it does not contain them. The era that holds all three is the Mesozoic.

choices.text: An epoch inside the Paleozoic Era
choices.rationale: Both parts are off. The Jurassic is a period, not an epoch, and the Paleozoic holds older periods such as the Permian and Cambrian.

questions.explanation: Each name on the time scale has a rank. The Jurassic is a period, and periods are grouped into eras. Reading the table shows the Jurassic in the middle of the Mesozoic Era, between the Triassic and the Cretaceous.
questions.misconception: Every famous time name (like Jurassic) is an era, or the Jurassic is part of the most recent era.

questions.misconception: Because the Phanerozoic fills most of a typical time-scale chart, it must be most of Earth's history.
questions.hint: Divide the Phanerozoic's length by all of Earth's history, then multiply by 100.

choices.text: It lasted longer than the three earlier eons put together
choices.rationale: The graph shows the opposite: about 541 million years for the Phanerozoic versus about 4,059 million for the three earlier eons combined.

choices.text: Its fossil-rich, well-preserved rocks allow many named units
choices.rationale: Correct. Phanerozoic rocks are better preserved and full of fossils, so geologists have split this eon into many named eras, periods and epochs, and charts stretch it to fit them. The chart is not to scale.

choices.text: Nothing worth recording happened before it began
choices.rationale: Earth formed, the moon formed, oceans and an atmosphere appeared, and life began and produced oxygen, all before the Phanerozoic.

choices.text: It is the eon we live in, so charts treat it as most important
choices.rationale: Charts don't size units by how much they matter to people. They make room for the many named units that the Phanerozoic's fossil-rich, well-preserved rocks allow.

questions.explanation: Time-scale charts are usually drawn for readability, not to scale. The Phanerozoic has abundant fossils of shelled animals and plants and more well-preserved rock, so geologists have named many units within it, and those names need room. questions.prompt: On this lesson's time scale, the Cambrian Period lasted about 56 million years (541 to 485 Ma), but the Silurian lasted only about 25 million years (444 to 419 Ma). Why aren't geologic periods all the same length?
questions.accessiblePrompt: On this lesson's time scale, the Cambrian Period lasted about 56 million years, from 541 to 485 million years ago, but the Silurian Period lasted only about 25 million years, from 444 to 419 million years ago. Why are geologic periods not all the same length?

choices.text: They were meant to be equal, but older dates were measured poorly
choices.rationale: Geologists never set out to make equal blocks. Even with perfect dates, the periods would still differ, because each boundary follows a real change in the record.

choices.text: A new period starts every time a fresh layer of sediment is laid down
choices.rationale: Sediment layers form all the time, often many in a single year, so this would make periods tiny and countless.

choices.text: Each period matches one full cycle of ice sheets advancing and retreating
choices.rationale: Glacial cycles last tens of thousands of years, far shorter than periods, and many periods had no big ice sheets at all.

choices.text: Their edges follow major rock and fossil changes, which came unevenly
choices.rationale: Correct. Boundaries are placed where the record shows major change, such as a mass extinction, and those events did not arrive on a schedule.

questions.explanation: Geologists don't chop Earth's history into equal pieces like a calendar. They draw boundaries where the rock and fossil record changes sharply, for example where many kinds of fossils vanish in a mass extinction or new kinds appear. Those events were spaced unevenly, so the periods between them have uneven lengths.
questions.misconception: Geologic periods are equal-length blocks of time, like months on a calendar.
questions.hint: What does the lesson say scientists use to mark the end of one span of time and the start of the next?

questions.prompt: In a tall cliff, many kinds of shelled fossils appear layer after layer, then stop at one level. In the layers higher up, most of those kinds never show up again. Cliffs on other continents show the same kinds stopping at a layer of the same age. What does this pattern most likely record?
questions.accessiblePrompt: In a tall cliff, many kinds of shelled fossils appear in layer after layer, then stop at one level. In the layers higher up the cliff, most of those kinds never appear again. Cliffs on other continents show the same kinds of fossils stopping at a layer of the same age. What does this pattern most likely record?
questions.conditions: The layers are undisturbed. The rock type is the same just below and just above the level where the fossils stop, so the local setting did not change. The layers on either side of that level were laid down one right after the other, with no gap in time.

choices.text: Many species died out within a short time: a mass extinction
choices.rationale: Correct. Many unrelated kinds vanish at the same level in many places and never return, so the simplest explanation is that they died out together over a short span.

choices.text: The animals moved away and kept living somewhere else
choices.rationale: If they had only moved, their fossils would turn up in younger layers somewhere else. The same kinds vanish at the same level on several continents, so they were gone everywhere.

choices.text: The layers higher in the cliff are older than the ones lower down
choices.rationale: In undisturbed layers the reverse is true: lower layers formed first, so higher layers are younger.

choices.text: Each species slowly changed into a new species over millions of years
choices.rationale: Slow change would show up gradually across many layers, not as many different kinds stopping together at a single level.

questions.explanation: Fossils record which organisms were living when each layer formed. When many unrelated kinds disappear at the same level in many places and stay missing in younger layers, the record shows a mass extinction. One cliff alone could reflect a local change, such as a sea drying up; finding the same disappearance at matching layers around the world is what marks a mass extinction, and geologists use it to place a boundary on the time scale.
questions.misconception: A sudden disappearance of fossils means the animals moved away or slowly turned into other species.
questions.hint: If a fossil kind never appears in any younger layer, what happened to those living things?

questions.prompt: Scientists rely mainly on meteorites, rather than Earth's own rocks, to find out when Earth formed. Which reasons support this choice? Select all that apply.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Scientists rely mainly on meteorites, which are space rocks that fell to Earth, rather than Earth's own rocks, to find out when Earth formed. Which reasons support this choice? Select all that apply.

choices.text: They formed with Earth, out of the same cloud of gas and dust
choices.rationale: Correct. Asteroids and planets grew out of the same collapsing cloud of gas and dust at about the same time, so the oldest meteorites date the start of the whole system.

choices.text: Earth's first rocks have been worn away or recycled since
choices.rationale: Correct. Weathering and plate tectonics have destroyed or reworked Earth's earliest rocks, so none survive from the very start.

choices.text: A meteorite's age tells the date it crashed into Earth's surface
choices.rationale: The Canyon Diablo meteorite landed only about 50,000 years ago, but its material is about 4.6 billion years old. Its age is when it formed, not when it fell.

choices.text: Meteorites hold fossils of the very first life on Earth
choices.rationale: The meteorites used for dating are pieces of asteroids, not Earth rock, so they hold no fossils of Earth life. Their value is their age.

questions.explanation: The planets and the asteroids grew out of the same spinning cloud, so meteorites that come from asteroids are samples of the solar system's building material. Earth can't give that date directly, because weathering and plate tectonics have destroyed its first rocks. Absolute dating of meteorites gives about 4.6 billion years.
questions.misconception: A meteorite's age is the date it landed, or Earth's oldest rocks still record its birth.
questions.hint: Think about where meteorites come from, and what has happened to Earth's surface over billions of years.

questions.prompt: Young Earth was hot enough that much of it was molten. Why did this lead to a planet with an iron-rich core at its center and lighter rock near its surface?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Young Earth was hot enough that much of it was molten, meaning melted rock. Why did this lead to a planet with an iron-rich core at its center and lighter rock near its surface?

choices.text: Iron arrived later in meteorites and was buried by volcanoes
choices.rationale: Iron was part of Earth's starting material. The core formed when that iron separated out, not when extra iron was delivered and buried.

choices.text: The great heat turned silicon deep inside into iron
choices.rationale: Heating melts and moves materials, but it does not change one element into another.

choices.text: Dense iron and nickel sank while lighter materials rose
choices.rationale: Correct. Melting let materials move, so the densest sank toward the center and lighter ones, like silicon and aluminum, moved up toward the surface.

choices.text: The core was built first, and the rest was added on top later
choices.rationale: Scientists think young Earth started with about the same mix all the way through. The layers separated afterward, while it was molten.

choices.text: The oxygen kept reacting with iron in seawater and sediment
choices.rationale: Correct. The rusty iron layers are the evidence: oxygen was being used up in reactions until those iron supplies ran low.

choices.text: Oxygen is too heavy a gas to escape from the ocean into the air
choices.rationale: Gases move between water and air all the time. The oxygen was not trapped by its weight; it was being used up in reactions.

choices.rationale: Land plants came much later. Ocean cyanobacteria were already making oxygen long before any plants grew on land.

questions.explanation: Oxygen reacts readily with iron. questions.misconception: Oxygen made by living things goes straight into the air, or it is stored somewhere as gas rather than used up in reactions.
questions.hint: The red bands are a clue. What happens to iron when it meets oxygen?

The fossil record shows new species appearing after extinctions again and again.

questions.prompt: Scientists keep what they observe separate from how they explain it. Sort each statement as an observation (evidence) or an explanation (hypothesis).
questions.accessiblePrompt: Scientists keep what they observe separate from how they explain it. Sort each statement into one of two groups: an observation, meaning evidence that can be measured or seen, or an explanation, meaning a hypothesis about what happened.

items.text: Moon rocks have a makeup very close to Earth's mantle
items.rationale: Observation: chemists measured this in rock samples brought back by astronauts.

items.text: A Mars-sized body hit young Earth, and the debris formed the moon
items.rationale: Explanation: no one saw this; it is the giant impact hypothesis, built to fit the moon-rock evidence.

items.text: Lab dating shows the Canyon Diablo meteorite is about 4.6 billion years old
items.rationale: Observation: the meteorite's age is measured in the lab by absolute dating.

items.text: The sun and planets grew from a spinning cloud of gas and dust
items.rationale: Explanation: no one watched the solar system form; the nebular hypothesis is built to fit evidence such as the ages of meteorites.

items.text: Stromatolite fossils are found in rocks about 3.5 billion years old
items.rationale: Observation: the fossils and the age of their rocks can be studied directly.

items.text: Oxygen released by cyanobacteria caused the first big rise of oxygen in the air
items.rationale: Explanation: scientists infer this cause-and-effect link from stromatolites, banded iron layers and other rock evidence.

questions.explanation: Observations are things that can be measured or seen today, such as a rock's makeup or the age of a meteorite or fossil. Explanations connect those observations into a story of what happened, such as a giant impact or a collapsing cloud of gas and dust. Strong explanations fit many observations, but they remain explanations and can be revised when new evidence appears.
questions.misconception: An explanation that most scientists accept is the same thing as an observation.
questions.hint: Could someone measure or see it directly today, or is it a story that ties the measurements together?

questions.prompt: The layers in a canyon wall show which ones formed first, but not how many years ago. Which added evidence would let scientists attach ages in years to these layers?
questions.accessiblePrompt: The rock layers in a canyon wall show which layers formed first, but not how many years ago they formed. Which added evidence would let scientists attach ages in years to these layers?
questions.conditions: The canyon's layers are undisturbed sedimentary rocks, such as sandstone, shale and limestone.

choices.text: Counting the layers, since each one took one year to form
choices.rationale: Layers build up at very different rates: one flood can leave a thick layer in days, while a thin one can take thousands of years. In rocks like these, counting layers gives their order, not their ages; only special layers, such as yearly lake-bottom layers, can be counted as years.

choices.text: Measuring how thick each layer is, since thicker ones took longer
choices.rationale: Thickness alone gives no age. Without knowing how fast the sediment piled up, a thickness can't be turned into years, and those rates vary hugely.

choices.text: Checking the size of the fossils, since older animals were smaller
choices.rationale: Fossil size says nothing about age in years; large and small animals lived in every era. Fossils help match and order layers, not give them numeric ages.

choices.text: Absolute dating of volcanic ash found between the layers
choices.rationale: Correct. Volcanic ash is a material that absolute dating can measure. A dated ash bed is younger than the layers under it and older than the layers on top of it, so it sets limits on their ages in years; two dated ash beds bracket the layers between them.

questions.explanation: Rock layers and fossils give relative ages: they show which came first. To put numbers on them, scientists use absolute dating, which works on certain materials such as volcanic ash, lava, meteorites and moon rocks. Dated ash beds above and below a sedimentary layer bracket its age, for example between 75 and 72 million years ago.
questions.misconception: Rock layers can be given ages in years just by counting them, measuring their thickness or looking at their fossils.
questions.hint: Which materials in this lesson were given ages in years, and what kind of rock can be dated that way?

questions.prompt: Squeeze Earth's 4,600-million-year history into one 24-hour day: Earth forms at the first midnight and today arrives at the next one. How many minutes before that final midnight do the non-bird dinosaurs die out, 66 million years ago? Round to the nearest minute.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Imagine squeezing Earth's whole history, about 4,600 million years, into one 24-hour day. Earth forms at the first midnight, and today arrives at the next midnight. How many minutes before that final midnight do the dinosaurs other than birds die out, 66 million years ago? Round to the nearest whole minute.
questions.limitations: The model keeps only the relative timing of events. Earth's age is the textbook's rounded 4.6 billion years; the U.S. Geological Survey's 4.54 billion years gives about 20.9 minutes, which still rounds to 21.
questions.workedSolution: 66 million years ÷ 4,600 million years = 0.0143 of Earth's history. A day has 24 × 60 = 1,440 minutes, so 0.0143 × 1,440 minutes ≈ 20.7 minutes, which rounds to 21 minutes before midnight.
questions.explanation: On this model each minute stands for about 3.2 million years. The non-bird dinosaurs die out only about 21 minutes before midnight, the Cambrian Explosion comes a little under 3 hours before midnight, and modern humans arrive only a few seconds before it. Animals with shells and bones crowd into the last few hours of Earth's day.
questions.misconception: Familiar events such as the end of the dinosaurs fill a large share of Earth's history, as they seem to on many charts.
questions.hint: What fraction of Earth's history is 66 million years? Take that fraction of the 1,440 minutes in a day.

questions.prompt: The nebular hypothesis is the leading explanation for how the solar system formed. Put its steps in order, from first to last.
questions.accessiblePrompt: The nebular hypothesis is the leading explanation for how the solar system formed. Put these four steps of the hypothesis in order, from the first step to the last step.

items.text: Larger clumps pull in more material with their stronger gravity
items.rationale: Third: once clumps exist, the bigger ones have more gravity, so they sweep up still more dust and grow faster.

items.text: A huge cloud of gas and dust begins to contract and spin
items.rationale: First: everything starts with the cloud, called a nebula, pulling inward and spinning into a disk.

items.text: Planets have formed, and leftover rocky clumps remain as asteroids
items.rationale: Last: growing clumps become planets, and pieces that never joined a planet stay behind as asteroids.

items.text: Dust grains in the spinning disk collide and stick together
items.rationale: Second: inside the spinning disk, dust grains bump into one another and clump, the first step toward bigger bodies.

questions.explanation: In the nebular hypothesis, gas and dust in a huge cloud pull inward and spin into a disk. Dust grains collide and stick, and as clumps grow their stronger gravity pulls in even more material, until planets form. Clumps that never joined a planet remain as asteroids, which is why meteorites from asteroids can date the birth of the solar system.
questions.misconception: The planets appeared all at once, already full-sized, rather than growing step by step from dust.
questions.hint: Each step needs the one before it. What has to exist before clumps can start to grow?
